summaries.example: Imagine a snack that tastes pleasant. Does that automatically make it good? One philosopher might say yes, while another might say we still need to think about kindness, fairness, or harm. This shows the question at the heart of the debate: can facts we study about the world fully explain moral facts?
summaries.summary: Moral non-naturalism is a family of views about what moral facts are. Its best-known form says that properties such as goodness and wrongness are real, but they are not identical to, or fully reducible to, natural properties. Natural properties are features usually connected with science, observation, causes, or the physical and mental world. The entry explains that philosophers disagree about exactly what counts as natural, so there is no single simple definition of the natural/non-natural boundary. Non-naturalism is different from views that say moral talk only expresses feelings, and from views that say there are no moral facts. Supporters often use the Open Question Argument: even after learning that something is pleasant or useful, it can still seem reasonable to ask whether it is good. They also discuss moral intuition, the connection between moral judgment and action, and the idea that moral facts depend on natural facts. Critics say non-naturalism may make moral knowledge and motivation mysterious. The entry presents these arguments as an ongoing philosophical debate rather than a settled question.
key_ideas: Non-naturalists think moral properties are real but cannot simply be identified with scientific or other natural properties.
The Open Question Argument asks whether something can have a natural feature, such as being pleasant, without our having settled that it is good.
Moral intuitionism tries to explain how people can know moral truths.
Critics ask how non-natural moral facts could explain our beliefs, motivate us, or depend on natural facts.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate asks a basic question: what are we talking about when we say that something is good, bad, right, or wrong? The answer may affect how we think about science, feelings, reasons, and moral disagreement. Studying the debate also teaches us to separate different questions: what moral words mean, whether moral facts exist, how we know them, and how they guide action.

important_terms.definition: A view in moral philosophy that says moral properties, such as goodness or wrongness, are not the same as ordinary natural properties studied by science.
The idea that there are real moral facts, not just personal feelings or commands.
A property is reducible when it can be completely explained as another property. Non-reductionists deny that moral properties can be explained this way.
The idea that moral understanding may come partly from directly recognizing that an action is right or wrong, somewhat like noticing a color.
The idea that two situations cannot differ morally unless they differ in some natural or non-moral way.

questions_to_think_about: Does something being pleasant always make it good?
How might someone recognize that an action is wrong?
Can two actions be exactly alike in every non-moral way but different in moral value?
Should science be the only guide to what is real?

summaries.example: Suppose a government policy causes serious suffering, but someone argues that the policy is acceptable because it produces economic growth. A non-naturalist might say that the policy’s moral wrongness is a real feature, not identical to suffering, growth, or any other natural feature, even though those facts help determine the moral assessment. A naturalist might instead argue that the moral property is itself a natural property or is reducible to natural facts. The disagreement concerns both metaphysics and explanation.
summaries.summary: Moral non-naturalism is not one completely uniform doctrine. In meta-ethics, it can concern the meaning of moral predicates, the way moral knowledge is acquired, or—most often—the nature of moral properties. On the main metaphysical version, moral properties are real but are not identical with or reducible to natural properties. The entry emphasizes that “natural” has many proposed meanings, including being studied by science, having causal powers, appearing in natural laws, or being knowable only through experience. None is presented as the final definition. The discussion begins with Moore’s so-called naturalistic fallacy. Moore’s deeper concern is not merely the form of an inference but the attempt to define or reduce goodness to something else. His Open Question Argument claims that any proposed naturalistic analysis leaves room for a competent speaker to ask whether the analyzed feature is really moral. The argument may support anti-reductionism, but it does not by itself rule out naturalists who regard moral properties as natural and irreducible, nor does it defeat every alternative theory of meaning. Non-naturalists commonly appeal to intuitionism, yet this raises questions about reliability, causal access, and how moral concepts refer to their objects. Further objections ask whether moral properties explain our beliefs, how they motivate action, and why moral facts necessarily depend on natural or non-moral facts. The entry concludes that the debate also reflects different philosophical methods: preserving ordinary moral appearances versus prioritizing scientific explanatory standards.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes several uses of “non-naturalism”: semantic, epistemological, and metaphysical. The metaphysical use is treated as the main one.
The natural/non-natural distinction is itself contested. Proposed tests involve science, causation, laws of nature, a priori knowledge, or explanatory roles.
Moore’s Open Question Argument may challenge reductionist naturalism, but it does not automatically defeat naturalism that treats moral properties as natural yet irreducible.
Intuitionism offers a route to moral knowledge, but critics ask how intuitions could reliably track properties that are causally isolated from the natural world.
Non-naturalism faces challenges about explaining moral beliefs, motivation, and the dependence of moral facts on non-moral facts.
Methodological disagreement matters: non-naturalists give weight to common moral thinking, while opponents often emphasize fit with scientific explanation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue reaches beyond a technical dispute about labels. It concerns whether moral truths are part of reality, whether science can explain all that matters, and how reasons for action fit into the world. It also clarifies several distinctions that are often blurred: moral realism versus anti-realism, naturalism versus non-naturalism, and reductionism versus anti-reductionism. Understanding those distinctions helps readers evaluate arguments without treating one objection as a solution to every problem.

important_terms.definition: A meta-ethical family of views holding, most commonly, that moral properties exist but are not identical with or reducible to natural properties.
The metaphysical thesis that moral properties are real and not reducible to natural properties, in a relevant sense of “natural.”

A disputed label for the inference from purely factual premises to a moral conclusion. The entry argues that the issue is better understood as a dispute about reduction than as a standard logical fallacy.
Moore’s argument that a naturalistic definition of a moral term leaves a question such as “It is pleasant, but is it good?” apparently open to a competent speaker.
The view that moral knowledge involves direct or quasi-perceptual recognition of moral properties or truths.
A relation in which moral differences require some difference in natural or non-moral facts, although the reverse need not hold.

The claim that moral judgment has a necessary or rational connection to motivation. A weaker version says that judging an action morally required should motivate an agent unless the agent is practically irrational.
An approach that rejects moral facts altogether, often claiming either that moral claims express attitudes or that moral predicates fail to refer to genuine properties.

questions_to_think_about: Does the apparent openness of “It is pleasant, but is it good?” show that goodness is not identical to pleasantness, or could it reflect limits in what speakers know?
Can a property be irreducible without being non-natural? Why does the entry separate these ideas?
If moral properties do not cause our intuitions, what could make moral intuition reliable?
Why might supervenience seem easier for a naturalist to explain than for a non-naturalist?
Which should receive more weight in meta-ethics: common moral judgment or a theory that fits scientific explanation?

summaries.example: A school chooses between two plans. Plan A is enjoyable but leaves one student out; Plan B is less exciting but includes everyone. Someone might say that enjoyment makes Plan A good. Another person may agree that it is enjoyable but still ask whether it is good overall. That extra question resembles the Open Question Argument. It suggests that “enjoyable” and “good” may not mean the same thing, though philosophers debate whether this really proves anything about the nature of goodness.
summaries.summary: Moral non-naturalism is a group of theories about moral reality. Its central idea is that properties such as goodness and wrongness are real, but they are not identical to, or fully explainable in terms of, natural properties. Natural properties might be the kinds of features studied by science, involved in causes, or described by the best account of the physical and mental world. The entry stresses that philosophers do not agree on one definition of “natural,” so non-naturalism cannot be explained by a single easy test. It is also important to keep non-naturalism separate from other positions. Moral realists say there are moral truths; non-cognitivists treat moral language mainly as the expression of attitudes; error theorists say moral claims aim at facts but there are no such facts. The entry gives special attention to Moore’s arguments. The so-called naturalistic fallacy is really aimed at the idea that goodness can be reduced to something else. The Open Question Argument says that if “good” meant exactly the same as “pleasant,” then asking whether a pleasant thing is good would be like asking whether an unmarried bachelor is unmarried. Yet critics reply that people may understand a word without knowing the theory that best explains its use. They also point out that the argument may oppose reduction rather than every form of naturalism. Non-naturalists often use intuitionism to explain moral knowledge. Critics then ask how intuitions can reliably reveal non-natural properties, especially if those properties do not cause our thoughts. Other challenges concern explanation, motivation, and supervenience: moral differences seem to require differences in non-moral facts. The entry presents these as serious but contested problems.
key_ideas: Non-naturalism usually says that moral properties exist but cannot be reduced to natural properties.
Philosophers disagree about what “natural” means, so the debate is partly about how to draw the boundary.
The Open Question Argument appears to challenge definitions such as “good means pleasant,” but critics say a word’s meaning may not be obvious to every competent speaker.
Intuitionism tries to explain moral knowledge, while critics ask how moral intuitions could be dependable.
The theory must address why moral facts seem tied to natural facts and why moral judgments can guide behavior.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate helps us ask what moral claims are, how we could know them, and why they should matter for action. It also shows why philosophical arguments need careful definitions. Saying that morality is “not natural” might concern meaning, knowledge, or the existence of properties, and those are different claims. Sorting them out makes disagreements clearer and prevents quick arguments from doing more work than they can support.

important_terms.definition: A group of views saying that moral features are real but are not simply the same as ordinary natural features such as pleasure, behavior, or physical facts.
The belief that moral statements can express truths about how things really are.
The claim that one kind of property can be explained completely in terms of another kind of property.
Moore’s challenge to definitions of goodness: even if something has the proposed natural feature, it can still seem sensible to ask whether it is good.
A theory that explains moral knowledge as a kind of direct recognition or awareness of moral truths.
The idea that a moral change requires some change in the natural or non-moral facts, even though natural changes do not always create moral changes.
The view that moral judgments are connected to motivation, at least for people who are rational and understand what they are judging.

questions_to_think_about: If something is useful, does that settle whether it is good?
Could moral intuition be like noticing a fact, or is it more like having a feeling?
Why would a non-naturalist want to separate moral properties from scientific properties?
What might make a moral judgment motivating for one person but not another?
Is it possible for two situations to match in every ordinary fact but differ morally?
